title: A lamp for my feet (Psalm 119:105)
hookLine: people memorize a verse to carry it in the dark

lines: A PHONE FLASHLIGHT ON A DARK PATH.
A CLAY LAMP IN YOUR PALM.
cards: Ever walked a dark path at night with only your phone's flashlight? A camping trip, a power cut, a country road. The light doesn't show you the whole way.
It shows the next two steps: a root, a puddle, the edge of the path. And that turns out to be enough. You keep walking, two steps at a time.

Now an older kind of light: a little clay oil lamp, small enough to hold in your palm, with a wick and a tiny flame. In ancient Israel, people carried lamps like that at night. It didn't light up the road ahead.
It lit your feet. Today's word comes from someone who knew that kind of light.

teach.h: NOT A FLOODLIGHT: THE NEXT STEP.
teach.b: Here it is, from Psalm 119, in the King James Bible: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." Not a floodlight. Not a map of the next ten years.
Enough light for the next step. That's the psalm's picture of God's word: not seeing everything, but not walking blind. Psalm 119, a hundred and seventy-six verses long, is built like a puzzle.
In Hebrew it's an alphabet poem: twenty-two sections, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and in each section all eight verses begin with that letter.
Our verse opens the section for the letter nun, and the Hebrew word for lamp, ner, starts with it. Verse after verse names God's word in some form: law, statutes, precepts, commandments.
The poet says it outright: "O how love I thy law!"

teach.h: THY WORD HAVE I HID IN MINE HEART.
teach.b: Earlier in the same psalm is a line that explains why people memorize verses at all: "Thy word have I hid in mine heart." Hid, as in stored away. Jews and Christians both learn verses by heart.
A verse learned by heart goes where a book can't: into a hospital bed, a prison cell, a sleepless night, a moment with no phone and no light.
It's a lamp you don't have to find in the dark.

how: Some Christians memorize Bible verses, often starting in childhood Sunday school, and repeat them in hard moments.

o: a path, the road ahead in the dark
a small oil lamp you hold in your hand
a law, one of God's commandments

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: enough light for the next step

s: an ancient lamp lit the whole road ahead
a small clay oil lamp lit your feet: the next step or two.
twenty-two sections, one for each Hebrew letter, eight verses each.
in Psalm 119, the law is only a rulebook
the poet says outright, "O how love I thy law!"

games.q: you're walking home on a dark country road. all you have is a small light that shows two steps ahead. what do you do?
o: keep walking, two steps at a time.
games.why: that's the psalm's picture: "a lamp unto my feet." not the whole road, just enough to take the next step.

practice: Say the first half slowly, thy word is a lamp unto my feet, then the second, and a light unto my path, a few times each, letting each phrase land on a breath.
Then put them together and keep repeating the whole verse quietly, without rushing. If you pray, make it a prayer; if you don't, just let it settle in.
